notes.h: Antenatal care: booking, screening and routine surveillance
notes.body:
Antenatal care aims to keep healthy pregnancies healthy, pick up complications early and support informed choice. NICE antenatal guidance (2021) recommends booking ideally by 10 weeks. An uncomplicated pregnancy usually has about 10 appointments for a nulliparous woman and about 7 for a parous woman.

Booking visit:
- History: previous pregnancies, medical conditions, medicines, mental health, social risk, and a domestic abuse enquiry asked when the woman is alone.
- BMI, blood pressure, urinalysis, and a midstream urine to screen for asymptomatic bacteriuria.
- Bloods: full blood count, blood group and antibodies, screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis, and sickle cell and thalassaemia screening, offered by 10 weeks so partner testing can be done early. Rubella screening is no longer routine in England.
- Risk assessment for pre-eclampsia (low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks if at increased risk), gestational diabetes, VTE and fetal growth restriction.
- Advice: folic acid until 12 weeks (a higher dose if at increased risk of neural tube defects), vitamin D, smoking cessation with carbon monoxide testing, and no alcohol.

Screening timeline:
- Dating scan at 11+2 to 14+1 weeks, measuring crown–rump length. The combined test (nuchal translucency, PAPP-A and hCG) gives the chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13.
- Quadruple test, 14+2 to 20+0 weeks: screens for trisomy 21 only.
- A higher-chance result (1 in 150 or greater) leads to an offer of NIPT (cell-free DNA screening) or a diagnostic test. Diagnostic options are chorionic villus sampling from 11 weeks or amniocentesis from 15 weeks.
- Fetal anomaly scan at 18+0 to 20+6 weeks.
- Oral glucose tolerance test at 24–28 weeks if risk factors are present: BMI above 30, a previous baby of 4.5 kg or more, previous gestational diabetes, a first-degree relative with diabetes, or a high-risk family origin.
- RhD-negative women: routine anti-D prophylaxis in the third trimester, plus anti-D after sensitising events. Cell-free fetal DNA testing can show the fetus is RhD-negative, so anti-D can be avoided.

From 24 weeks, symphysis–fundal height is measured and plotted on a customised chart. Blood pressure and urine are checked at every visit. Vaccines offered in pregnancy are pertussis (ideally 16–32 weeks), influenza, RSV (from 28 weeks) and COVID-19 as currently recommended.

Worked example: by Naegele's rule, LMP 1 March 2026 + 9 months + 7 days gives an EDD of 8 December 2026. The dating scan overrides this.

Pitfalls: NIPT is screening, not diagnosis. The quadruple test does not cover trisomies 18 or 13. New hypertension after 20 weeks needs same-day pre-eclampsia assessment.

notes.h: Labour and delivery: stages, progress, monitoring and operative birth
notes.body:
Labour is regular painful contractions with progressive cervical change. Progress depends on the three Ps: power (contractions), passenger (size, presentation, position and attitude) and passage (pelvis and soft tissues).

Stages (NICE intrapartum care):
- Latent first stage: painful contractions with cervical change, up to 4 cm.
- Established first stage: regular painful contractions with progressive dilatation from 4 cm. Delay is suspected with less than 2 cm in 4 hours, or slowing progress in a parous woman. Manage with amniotomy, reassessment, then oxytocin if delay is confirmed.
- Second stage: full dilatation to birth, with a passive phase and an active pushing phase. Birth is expected within about 3 hours of active pushing in a first labour, and about 2 hours in later labours.
- Third stage: birth to delivery of the placenta and membranes. Active management (a prophylactic uterotonic, deferred cord clamping and controlled cord traction) reduces haemorrhage. The third stage is prolonged beyond 30 minutes with active management, or 60 minutes with physiological management.

Mechanism of an occipito-anterior birth: engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension (crowning), restitution, external rotation, then delivery of the shoulders and body.

Fetal monitoring: intermittent auscultation if low risk, and continuous CTG if risk factors are present or arise. NICE fetal monitoring guidance (2022) stresses the whole clinical picture and the trend over time.
- Normal features: baseline 110–160 bpm, variability 5–25 bpm, accelerations.
- Concerning features: late decelerations, reduced variability, a rising baseline or a sinusoidal pattern.

Induction: the Bishop score (dilatation, length, consistency, position, station) guides the method. A score of 6 or less is unfavourable and needs ripening with prostaglandin or a balloon catheter. Above 6, amniotomy and oxytocin may be used. Offer a membrane sweep, and offer induction from 41+0 weeks (NICE NG207).

Operative birth:
- Assisted vaginal birth (ventouse or forceps) requires full dilatation, ruptured membranes, a known position, a head no more than 1/5 palpable abdominally, analgesia and an empty bladder.
- Caesarean categories:
  - Category 1: immediate threat to the life of woman or fetus; birth ideally within 30 minutes.
  - Category 2: compromise that is not immediately life-threatening; birth within 75 minutes.
  - Category 3: early birth needed without compromise.
  - Category 4: timed to suit the woman and the service.

Perineal trauma grades:
- First degree: skin only.
- Second degree: perineal muscle.
- Third degree: anal sphincter. 3a is less than 50% of the external sphincter, 3b is more than 50%, and in 3c the internal sphincter is also torn.
- Fourth degree: extends into the anorectal mucosa.

Pitfalls: epidural prolongs the second stage and increases assisted vaginal birth but not caesarean birth. Exclude obstruction and malpresentation before starting oxytocin.

notes.h: Obstetric emergencies: haemorrhage, dystocia, cord prolapse, eclampsia and collapse
notes.body:
Emergencies are rehearsed as drills. Call for help early (senior obstetrician, midwife, anaesthetist, neonatologist), work through ABC and keep contemporaneous notes.

Postpartum haemorrhage (RCOG Green-top 52):
- Primary PPH: 500 ml or more within 24 hours of birth. It is minor at 500–1000 ml, and major above 1000 ml or with shock. Secondary PPH occurs from 24 hours to 12 weeks, often from retained tissue or endometritis.
- Causes (the four Ts): tone (atony, the commonest), trauma, tissue (retained products) and thrombin (coagulopathy).
- Resuscitation: two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch and coagulation tests, warmed fluids and blood products.
- Stop the bleeding: rub up a contraction, empty the bladder and apply bimanual compression. Uterotonics are oxytocin, ergometrine (avoid in hypertension), carboprost (avoid in asthma) and misoprostol, plus tranexamic acid.
- Escalation: balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, interventional radiology, then hysterectomy.

Shoulder dystocia: the anterior shoulder impacts behind the symphysis after the head is born, which may show as the "turtle sign".
- Stop pushing, and use McRoberts' position with suprapubic pressure.
- If these fail, use internal rotational manoeuvres, delivery of the posterior arm, or the all-fours position.
- Never use fundal pressure.
- Risks: brachial plexus injury (Erb's palsy, C5–C6), PPH and severe tears.

Cord prolapse: suspect it when fetal bradycardia follows membrane rupture, especially with a high or non-cephalic presenting part. Elevate the presenting part manually or by filling the bladder, and use the knee–chest or head-down left lateral position. Minimise handling of the cord. Arrange a Category 1 caesarean unless vaginal birth is imminent.

Eclampsia: seizures in pre-eclampsia. Give magnesium sulfate as the anticonvulsant, and monitor reflexes, respiratory rate and urine output for toxicity (antidote: calcium gluconate). Control blood pressure with labetalol, nifedipine or hydralazine. Deliver once the woman is stable. HELLP (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets) is a severe variant.

Antepartum haemorrhage (bleeding from 24 weeks):
- Abruption: painful bleeding with a tense, "woody" uterus. Bleeding may be concealed, so shock can exceed the visible loss.
- Placenta praevia: painless bleeding with a high or malpresenting fetus. No digital vaginal examination until praevia is excluded.
- Vasa praevia: bleeding at membrane rupture with acute fetal compromise.

Maternal collapse: from about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the aorta and vena cava. Use manual left uterine displacement during CPR. Without return of circulation, perform a resuscitative hysterotomy, aiming for birth within 5 minutes of arrest. This mainly aids maternal survival.

Pitfalls: visual estimates underestimate blood loss, so weigh swabs. Tachycardia and low urine output precede hypotension in young women. VTE has repeatedly been a leading direct cause of maternal death in MBRRACE-UK reports.

notes.h: Gynaecology: menstrual disorders, early pregnancy, menopause and cancers
notes.body:
Heavy menstrual bleeding (NICE NG88) is defined by its impact on quality of life.
- Check a full blood count, and arrange ultrasound if structural pathology is suspected.
- Without a structural cause, the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is first-line.
- Alternatives: tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic), NSAIDs, combined hormonal contraception or progestogens.
- Surgery: endometrial ablation, myomectomy or hysterectomy.

Endometriosis (NICE NG73) is endometrial-like tissue outside the uterus. It causes cyclical pelvic pain, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia and subfertility. Normal examination or imaging does not exclude it. Laparoscopy can diagnose and treat it. Medical options are analgesia, hormonal suppression and GnRH analogues.

Polycystic ovary syndrome (Rotterdam criteria, 2003) needs two of:
- oligo- or anovulation
- hyperandrogenism (clinical or biochemical)
- polycystic ovarian morphology
The 2023 international guideline permits anti-Müllerian hormone in place of ultrasound in adults. Exclude thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Long-term risks are type 2 diabetes, endometrial hyperplasia and cardiovascular disease. Letrozole (an aromatase inhibitor) is first-line for ovulation induction.

Early pregnancy (NICE NG126): pain or bleeding with a positive test is ectopic pregnancy until proven otherwise.
- Investigate with transvaginal ultrasound and serial hCG.
- Ectopic pregnancy is managed expectantly, with methotrexate (a folate antagonist) in selected stable women, or by laparoscopic salpingectomy.
- Miscarriage is managed expectantly, medically (mifepristone, an antiprogestogen, then misoprostol, a prostaglandin analogue) or surgically.
- Give anti-D to RhD-negative women where indicated, such as after surgical management.

Menopause (NICE NG23) is diagnosed clinically over 45 without FSH testing. Menopause before 40 is premature ovarian insufficiency. HRT must include a progestogen if the woman has a uterus, because unopposed oestrogen causes hyperplasia. Transdermal oestrogen carries a lower VTE risk than oral.

Cancers:
- Cervical: driven by high-risk HPV (especially 16 and 18). England screens ages 25–64 with primary HPV testing, and cytology is done only if HPV is positive. Since July 2025, HPV-negative women aged 25–49 in England are recalled every 5 years (previously 3), the same interval already used at 50–64. The adolescent HPV vaccination programme has been single-dose since September 2023; people who are immunosuppressed or living with HIV still need a multi-dose course.
- Endometrial: postmenopausal bleeding goes on an urgent suspected-cancer pathway with transvaginal ultrasound. Endometrial thickness of 4 mm or more prompts biopsy or hysteroscopy. Risk factors reflect unopposed oestrogen: obesity, nulliparity, PCOS, tamoxifen and Lynch syndrome.
- Ovarian: vague persistent symptoms (bloating, early satiety, pelvic pain, urinary frequency) prompt CA-125 testing, then ultrasound if raised. The Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI I) is U × M × CA-125, where U = 0, 1 or 3 (no, one, or two or more suspicious ultrasound features) and M = 1 if premenopausal or 3 if postmenopausal. NICE recommends specialist referral at an RMI of 250 or more.

Worked example: a 58-year-old with a single episode of postmenopausal bleeding and a 7 mm endometrium needs endometrial sampling.

Pitfalls: always do a pregnancy test in reproductive-age pain or bleeding. CA-125 also rises in endometriosis, fibroids and pregnancy.

notes.h: Sexual and reproductive health: contraception, STIs and consent
notes.body:
UK Medical Eligibility Criteria (UKMEC) grade each contraceptive method for each condition:
- 1: no restriction.
- 2: benefits generally outweigh risks.
- 3: risks generally outweigh benefits.
- 4: unacceptable risk.

Methods:
- LARC methods are the most effective because they do not depend on the user. The implant (progestogen, anovulatory) is the most effective reversible method. The levonorgestrel IUS mainly acts on cervical mucus and the endometrium. The copper IUD is non-hormonal. Injectable medroxyprogesterone delays the return of fertility and reduces bone density.
- Combined hormonal contraception inhibits ovulation. UKMEC 4 examples: migraine with aura, current or past VTE, current breast cancer, BP of 160/100 or above, and age 35 or over smoking 15 or more cigarettes a day.
- Progestogen-only pill: the traditional pill is late after 3 hours, desogestrel after 12 hours.
- Enzyme inducers (some antiepileptics, rifampicin) reduce efficacy of hormonal methods other than the IUS and injectable.

Emergency contraception (FSRH):
- Copper IUD: the most effective option. It can be fitted up to 120 hours after the first unprotected intercourse, or up to 5 days after the earliest likely ovulation.
- Ulipristal acetate, a selective progesterone receptor modulator, works up to 120 hours. Delay starting hormonal contraception for 5 days after taking it.
- Levonorgestrel is licensed up to 72 hours.

STIs (BASHH guidance):
- Chlamydia: the commonest diagnosed bacterial STI in the UK, often asymptomatic. Test by NAAT (vulvovaginal swab or first-void urine) and treat with doxycycline.
- Gonorrhoea: NAAT plus culture for sensitivities. Treat with ceftriaxone (a third-generation cephalosporin) and arrange a test of cure.
- Syphilis: a painless chancre (primary), then a rash including the palms and soles, and condylomata lata (secondary). Treat with benzathine penicillin and warn about the Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction.
- Herpes: painful ulcers, treated with aciclovir.
- Trichomonas: frothy discharge and a strawberry cervix, treated with metronidazole.
- Bacterial vaginosis (not an STI): fishy discharge, pH above 4.5 and clue cells. Candida gives itchy, curdy discharge with normal pH.
- Pelvic inflammatory disease: treat on clinical suspicion (pelvic pain with adnexal or cervical motion tenderness) to prevent infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
- HIV: start PEP as soon as possible, within 72 hours. PrEP is available through sexual health services. U=U: a sustained undetectable viral load means no sexual transmission.

Young people: under-16s can consent to contraception if Gillick competent, following Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986] and the Fraser guidelines. A child under 13 cannot consent to sexual activity (Sexual Offences Act 2003), so always follow safeguarding procedures.

Pitfalls: the implant is more effective than sterilisation. The copper IUD beats ulipristal, which beats levonorgestrel. Do not delay PID treatment for swab results.

notes.h: Neonatology: resuscitation, the newborn check, jaundice, breathing and infection
notes.body:
Most babies need only drying and warmth.

Newborn life support (Resuscitation Council UK):
- Delay cord clamping for at least 60 seconds in a well baby. Dry, wrap and keep warm; preterm babies go in a plastic bag under a radiant heater.
- Assess tone, breathing and heart rate. Heart rate best shows the baby's response.
- If the baby is not breathing adequately, put the head in a neutral position and give five inflation breaths, then ventilation breaths. Effective lung aeration corrects most bradycardia.
- If the heart rate stays below 60/min despite good ventilation, start compressions at a 3:1 ratio.

The Apgar score (appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration; 0–2 each) is recorded at 1, 5 and 10 minutes.

Newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE) is done within 72 hours and repeated at 6–8 weeks:
- Eyes: red reflex (cataract, retinoblastoma).
- Heart: murmurs and femoral pulses.
- Hips: Barlow and Ortolani tests, with ultrasound for abnormal findings or risk factors (breech presentation, family history).
- Testes: check for undescended testes.

The blood spot test around day 5 screens (in England) for ten conditions, including sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism, phenylketonuria and MCAD deficiency (MCADD). Tyrosinaemia type 1 was added in October 2025. Vitamin K is offered at birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

Jaundice (NICE CG98):
- Jaundice within 24 hours is always pathological. Think of haemolysis (rhesus or ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis) or sepsis.
- Physiological jaundice starts after 24 hours and settles within about 2 weeks.
- Prolonged jaundice lasts beyond 14 days at term or 21 days preterm. Measure conjugated bilirubin. Pale stools and dark urine suggest biliary atresia, which needs early Kasai surgery.
- Plot serum bilirubin against age in hours on threshold charts to guide phototherapy or exchange transfusion and prevent kernicterus.

Respiratory distress (tachypnoea, grunting, recession):
- Transient tachypnoea of the newborn: delayed fluid clearance, common after caesarean birth.
- Respiratory distress syndrome: surfactant deficiency in preterm babies. Antenatal corticosteroids reduce it, and it is treated with surfactant and respiratory support.
- Others: meconium aspiration, pneumothorax, congenital heart disease, infection.

Early-onset infection (NICE NG195): group B streptococcus is the leading cause. Risk factors include maternal GBS, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes and maternal fever. Red flags mean antibiotics within an hour; first-line is benzylpenicillin with gentamicin.

Complications of prematurity (birth before 37 weeks):
- intraventricular haemorrhage
- necrotising enterocolitis (feed intolerance, bilious aspirates, bloody stool, pneumatosis on X-ray)
- bronchopulmonary dysplasia
- retinopathy of prematurity
- patent ductus arteriosus

Worked example: a well, feeding 30-hour-old with jaundice is probably physiological. Still measure bilirubin and plot it; never rely on visual assessment.

Pitfalls: jaundice under 24 hours, bilious vomiting and pale stools are red flags.

notes.h: Child development: domains, milestones, red flags and assessment
notes.body:
Development is assessed in four domains:
- gross motor
- fine motor and vision
- speech, language and hearing
- social, emotional and behavioural

Primitive reflexes (Moro, grasp, asymmetric tonic neck) fade over the first months. If they persist, suspect neurological impairment such as cerebral palsy.

Learn milestones as a median age and a limit age, the age by which almost all children achieve the skill. Missing a limit age warrants assessment.

Key milestones (median, limit in brackets):
- Gross motor: head control at about 3 months. Sits unsupported at 6–8 months (9 months). Walks at about 12 months (18 months).
- Fine motor and vision: reaches at 4–5 months. Transfers objects at 6–7 months. Pincer grip at about 10 months (12 months). Tower of 3–4 bricks at 18 months. Copies a circle at 3 years and a cross at 4 years.
- Speech and language: polysyllabic babble at about 7 months. Words with meaning at about 12 months (no words by 18 months is a red flag). Two-word phrases at 2 years. Short sentences at 3 years.
- Social: social smile at about 6 weeks (8 weeks). Stranger wariness in the second half of the first year. Waves bye-bye at 10–12 months. Pretend play from 18 months to 2 years.

Red flags:
- Regression (loss of acquired skills) at any age. Assess urgently for neurodegenerative or metabolic disease.
- Hand preference before about 12 months, which suggests contralateral weakness (hemiplegia).
- Not walking by 18 months. In boys, check creatine kinase for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
- No speech by 18 months. Always test hearing.
- Abnormal tone, persistent primitive reflexes, or concern from parents.

Assessment:
- Correct for prematurity until about 2 years. A baby born at 28 weeks who is now 9 months old has a corrected age of 6 months.
- History: pregnancy, birth, family history, consanguinity and social circumstances.
- Examination: growth, head circumference, dysmorphism, neurocutaneous signs and neurology.
- Targeted tests: hearing and vision, thyroid function, creatine kinase, chromosomal microarray, fragile X testing and metabolic screening.
- A multidisciplinary child development team coordinates care.

Global delay has many causes: genetic conditions (Down syndrome, fragile X), cerebral palsy, congenital infection, metabolic disease, congenital hypothyroidism and neglect. Isolated speech delay suggests hearing loss or autism. Isolated motor delay suggests neuromuscular disease or cerebral palsy.

Cerebral palsy is a permanent, non-progressive disorder of movement and posture caused by injury to the developing brain. Spastic forms are the commonest.

Autism (NICE CG128) involves persistent social communication differences plus restricted, repetitive behaviours or interests. Refer to a specialist assessment team.

Pitfalls: quote limit ages when explaining when to worry. Correct for prematurity. Never dismiss regression as "a phase".

notes.h: Common childhood illness: fever, respiratory, gastrointestinal and serious infection
notes.body:
Children compensate well and then deteriorate quickly. Assess ABCDE using age-specific normal values.

Fever in under 5s (NICE NG143) uses a traffic-light system:
- An infant under 3 months with 38 °C or higher is high risk.
- An infant aged 3–6 months with 39 °C or higher is at least amber.
- A non-blanching rash, reduced consciousness, neck stiffness or seizure needs urgent assessment.

Respiratory:
- Bronchiolitis: usually RSV in infants, most often under 1. Coryza progresses to cough, wheeze and crackles. Care is supportive (oxygen, feeding support); bronchodilators, steroids and antibiotics are not recommended. Admit for apnoea, persistent hypoxaemia, marked distress or poor feeding.
- Croup: parainfluenza, about 6 months to 3 years. Barking cough and stridor. Give a single dose of oral corticosteroid; nebulised adrenaline is a bridge in severe cases.
- Epiglottitis: rare since Hib vaccination. Drooling, toxic appearance, tripod position. Do not examine the throat; secure the airway in theatre.
- Asthma: the 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN guideline diagnoses children aged 5 and over with objective tests (FeNO, spirometry with reversibility). Inhaled corticosteroids are the basis of preventer treatment. Life-threatening features: silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, saturations below 92%.

Gastrointestinal:
- Gastroenteritis (NICE CG84): distinguish dehydration from shock. Use oral rehydration solution for dehydration; give IV fluids for shock or failed oral rehydration.
- Pyloric stenosis: at 2–8 weeks, projectile non-bilious vomiting in a hungry baby. Gas shows hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Correct fluids and electrolytes before pyloromyotomy.
- Intussusception: 3 months to 2 years. Colicky pain with pallor, drawing up the legs, redcurrant jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass. Ultrasound shows a target sign; reduce with an air enema.
- Bilious vomiting in an infant means malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.

Serious infection:
- Meningococcal disease: give benzylpenicillin before hospital. In hospital, give a third-generation cephalosporin, adding amoxicillin under 3 months for Listeria. Dexamethasone is used in bacterial meningitis over 3 months.
- Kawasaki disease: fever for 5 days or more with conjunctivitis, rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, oral changes and hand or foot changes. Treat with IV immunoglobulin plus aspirin, a rare paediatric aspirin indication despite the Reye's syndrome risk. Echocardiography looks for coronary aneurysms.
- UTI (NICE NG224): refer infants under 3 months to paediatrics.
- Febrile seizures occur between 6 months and 5 years. A simple seizure is generalised, lasts under 15 minutes and does not recur within 24 hours.

Worked example: a well-looking 7-week-old with a temperature of 38.4 °C is still high risk. Admit for a septic screen and parenteral antibiotics.

Pitfalls: consider safeguarding (delayed presentation, inconsistent history, injuries in non-mobile infants). A mottled, drowsy child is seriously unwell whatever the temperature.

cards.f: By what gestation should booking ideally take place, and why?
cards.b: Ideally by 10 weeks, so that sickle cell and thalassaemia screening, partner testing and any diagnostic testing can be offered early in pregnancy.

cards.f: What is the window for the dating scan and the combined screening test?
cards.b: 11+2 to 14+1 weeks. Crown–rump length dates the pregnancy. Nuchal translucency is combined with PAPP-A and hCG to estimate the chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13.

cards.f: How does the quadruple test differ from the combined test?
cards.b: It is a blood-only test used from 14+2 to 20+0 weeks, when it is too late for the combined test. It screens for trisomy 21 only, not trisomies 18 or 13.

cards.f: What happens after a higher-chance screening result (1 in 150 or greater)?
cards.b: The woman is offered a choice: no further testing, NIPT (cell-free DNA screening, which is highly sensitive but still not diagnostic), or a diagnostic test (CVS or amniocentesis), which carries a small miscarriage risk.

cards.f: Compare chorionic villus sampling with amniocentesis.
cards.b: CVS samples placental tissue from about 11 weeks, which gives an earlier result. Amniocentesis samples amniotic fluid from 15 weeks. Both are diagnostic and carry a small procedure-related miscarriage risk; CVS can occasionally be confounded by confined placental mosaicism.

cards.f: List the NICE risk factors that prompt an OGTT for gestational diabetes.
cards.b: BMI above 30, a previous baby weighing 4.5 kg or more, previous gestational diabetes, a first-degree relative with diabetes, and a family origin with high diabetes prevalence. The test is done at 24–28 weeks, or earlier after previous GDM.

cards.f: What are the NICE diagnostic thresholds for gestational diabetes on an OGTT?
cards.b: A fasting plasma glucose of 5.6 mmol/L or more, or a 2-hour value of 7.8 mmol/L or more (the "5.6 and 7.8" rule).

cards.f: Why are RhD-negative women given anti-D, and when?
cards.b: Anti-D prevents maternal alloimmunisation against fetal RhD-positive cells, which would cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn in later pregnancies. It is given as routine prophylaxis in the third trimester and after sensitising events such as bleeding, trauma, ECV or procedures.

cards.f: Which vaccines are offered in pregnancy in the UK?
cards.b: Pertussis (ideally 16–32 weeks), seasonal influenza, RSV (from 28 weeks) and COVID-19 as currently recommended. Live vaccines such as MMR are avoided in pregnancy.

cards.f: Who should be offered low-dose aspirin in pregnancy, and from when?
cards.b: Women at increased risk of pre-eclampsia: those with one high-risk factor (for example chronic hypertension, previous hypertensive disease of pregnancy, CKD, diabetes or autoimmune disease) or two or more moderate factors. Aspirin is taken from 12 weeks until birth.

cards.f: Use Naegele's rule to calculate the EDD for an LMP of 10 January 2026.
cards.b: Add 9 months and 7 days: 10 October 2026 + 7 days = 17 October 2026. The rule assumes a regular 28-day cycle, and a dating scan takes precedence.

cards.f: Define the latent and established first stage of labour (NICE).
cards.b: The latent stage involves painful contractions with some cervical change, including effacement, up to 4 cm. The established first stage is regular painful contractions with progressive dilatation from 4 cm.

cards.f: When is delay in the established first stage suspected?
cards.b: When dilatation is less than 2 cm in 4 hours (in first or later labours), or when progress slows in a parous woman. Consider amniotomy, reassess after 2 hours, and seek obstetric review for oxytocin if delay is confirmed.

cards.f: List the cardinal movements of labour for an occipito-anterior position.
cards.b: Engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation, and expulsion of the shoulders and body.

cards.f: What does active management of the third stage involve, and what is its benefit?
cards.b: A prophylactic uterotonic, deferred cord clamping, and controlled cord traction after signs of separation. It reduces the risk of postpartum haemorrhage and the need for transfusion compared with physiological management.

cards.f: What are the five components of the Bishop score, and what does a low score mean?
cards.b: Cervical dilatation, length (effacement), consistency, position, and station of the presenting part. A score of 6 or less is unfavourable, and cervical ripening is needed before amniotomy.

cards.f: State the normal CTG baseline rate and variability.
cards.b: Baseline 110–160 bpm with variability of 5–25 bpm. Accelerations are reassuring.

cards.f: Contrast early, variable and late decelerations.
cards.b: Early decelerations mirror contractions and reflect head compression. Variable decelerations vary in timing and shape and reflect cord compression. Late decelerations begin after the contraction peak and return late, which suggests uteroplacental insufficiency and fetal hypoxia.

cards.f: Define caesarean section Categories 1 to 4.
cards.b: Category 1: immediate threat to the life of woman or fetus. Category 2: maternal or fetal compromise that is not immediately life-threatening. Category 3: no compromise, but early birth is needed. Category 4: birth timed to suit the woman and the service.

cards.f: What are the prerequisites for assisted vaginal birth?
cards.b: Full dilatation, ruptured membranes, a known fetal position, a head no more than 1/5 palpable abdominally and at or below the ischial spines, adequate analgesia, an empty bladder, a valid indication, consent and a back-up plan.

cards.f: Classify a perineal tear involving 60% of the external anal sphincter with the internal sphincter intact.
cards.b: A third-degree tear, subtype 3b (more than 50% of the external anal sphincter torn, internal sphincter intact). It needs repair in theatre by an experienced clinician.

cards.f: What effect does epidural analgesia have on labour outcomes?
cards.b: It gives the most effective pain relief. It is associated with a longer second stage and more assisted vaginal births, but not with higher caesarean rates or long-term backache.

cards.f: Define primary and secondary PPH.
cards.b: Primary PPH is blood loss of 500 ml or more from the genital tract within 24 hours of birth. Secondary PPH is abnormal or excessive bleeding between 24 hours and 12 weeks after birth.

cards.f: What are the four Ts of PPH, and which is commonest?
cards.b: Tone (uterine atony), trauma, tissue (retained products) and thrombin (coagulopathy). Atony is the commonest cause.

cards.f: Which uterotonics are contraindicated in hypertension and in asthma respectively?
cards.b: Ergometrine (an ergot alkaloid causing vasoconstriction) is avoided in hypertension and pre-eclampsia. Carboprost (a prostaglandin F2α analogue that can cause bronchospasm) is avoided in asthma.

cards.f: What are the first-line manoeuvres for shoulder dystocia?
cards.b: After calling for help and stopping pushing: McRoberts' position (hyperflexion of the hips) plus suprapubic pressure behind the anterior shoulder. Fundal pressure must never be used.

cards.f: Which nerve injury is classically associated with shoulder dystocia, and how does it present?
cards.b: Upper brachial plexus (C5–C6) injury, called Erb's palsy. The arm is adducted and internally rotated with the forearm pronated, the 'waiter's tip' posture.

cards.f: Give the immediate steps for umbilical cord prolapse.
cards.b: Call for help. Relieve compression by elevating the presenting part (manually or by filling the bladder), and use knee–chest or head-down left lateral positioning. Avoid handling the cord. Arrange urgent birth, usually Category 1 caesarean.

cards.f: What is magnesium sulfate used for in obstetrics, and how is toxicity recognised?
cards.b: It is used to prevent and treat eclamptic seizures, and for fetal neuroprotection in preterm birth. Toxicity causes loss of tendon reflexes, respiratory depression and reduced urine output; the antidote is calcium gluconate.

cards.f: Contrast placental abruption with placenta praevia.
cards.b: Abruption causes painful bleeding with a tender, hard uterus, possibly concealed loss and fetal distress. Praevia causes painless, often recurrent bleeding with a soft uterus and a high or malpresenting fetus, and digital vaginal examination must be avoided.

cards.f: Why is left uterine displacement used in maternal cardiac arrest?
cards.b: After about 20 weeks, the gravid uterus compresses the inferior vena cava and aorta, reducing venous return and the effectiveness of chest compressions. Manual displacement relieves this while CPR continues.

cards.f: When should resuscitative hysterotomy be performed?
cards.b: In maternal cardiac arrest from about 20 weeks with no return of spontaneous circulation. Aim to deliver within 5 minutes of arrest, mainly to improve maternal resuscitation.

cards.f: What is HELLP syndrome?
cards.b: A severe form of pre-eclampsia with haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets. It may present with epigastric or right upper quadrant pain, and the definitive treatment is birth.

cards.f: List the classic features of amniotic fluid embolism.
cards.b: Sudden maternal collapse in labour or soon after birth, with hypoxia, hypotension, seizures and often disseminated intravascular coagulation. It is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion, and treatment is supportive.

cards.f: What is first-line treatment for heavy menstrual bleeding with no structural or histological cause (NICE)?
cards.b: The levonorgestrel intrauterine system, if acceptable. Alternatives include tranexamic acid, NSAIDs, combined hormonal contraception and cyclical progestogens.

cards.f: State the Rotterdam criteria for PCOS.
cards.b: Two of three: oligo- or anovulation; clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism; and polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound. Other causes, such as thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia and non-classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia, must be excluded.

cards.f: What is first-line pharmacological ovulation induction in PCOS?
cards.b: Letrozole, an aromatase inhibitor that lowers oestrogen and so increases FSH via the feedback loop. It is offered alongside weight optimisation where relevant.

cards.f: Give the classic symptoms of endometriosis.
cards.b: Cyclical pelvic pain or dysmenorrhoea, deep dyspareunia, dyschezia, dysuria and subfertility. Normal examination and ultrasound do not exclude it.

cards.f: Which endometrial thickness on transvaginal ultrasound triggers further investigation in postmenopausal bleeding (standard UK practice)?
cards.b: 4 mm or more, which prompts endometrial sampling or hysteroscopy. Persistent or recurrent bleeding warrants investigation regardless of thickness.

cards.f: What is the Risk of Malignancy Index?
cards.b: RMI = U × M × CA-125. U is the ultrasound score: 0 for no suspicious features, 1 for one, 3 for two or more (multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites, metastases). M is 1 if premenopausal and 3 if postmenopausal. NICE recommends referral to a specialist gynaecological oncology team at an RMI of 250 or more.

cards.f: Which HPV types cause most cervical cancers, and how does England's screening programme test?
cards.b: High-risk types 16 and 18 cause most cases. England uses primary high-risk HPV testing, with cytology triage only for HPV-positive samples, from age 25 to 64. HPV-negative women are recalled every 5 years (extended from 3 years for ages 25–49 in July 2025).

cards.f: What are the management options for a tubal ectopic pregnancy?
cards.b: Expectant management in selected stable women with low and falling hCG. Medical management with methotrexate (a folate antagonist) in stable women meeting the criteria. Surgical management, usually laparoscopic salpingectomy, for rupture, instability, high hCG or a visible fetal heartbeat.

cards.f: How is menopause diagnosed according to NICE?
cards.b: Clinically, in women over 45 with typical vasomotor symptoms and either 12 months without a period, or irregular periods if perimenopausal. FSH testing is reserved for selected younger women, for example under 45 with suspected early menopause.

cards.f: Why must women with a uterus receive a progestogen with oestrogen HRT?
cards.b: Unopposed oestrogen stimulates the endometrium, raising the risk of hyperplasia and endometrial carcinoma. The progestogen protects the endometrium.

cards.f: Name risk factors for endometrial carcinoma.
cards.b: Factors that increase unopposed oestrogen exposure: obesity, nulliparity, early menarche or late menopause, PCOS, tamoxifen and oestrogen-only HRT. Lynch syndrome is a hereditary cause, and diabetes is also a risk factor.

cards.f: What do UKMEC categories 1–4 mean?
cards.b: 1: no restriction on use. 2: advantages generally outweigh risks. 3: risks generally outweigh advantages, so use only with specialist judgement. 4: unacceptable health risk.

cards.f: Give four UKMEC 4 conditions for combined hormonal contraception.
cards.b: Any four of: migraine with aura; current or past VTE; current breast cancer; blood pressure of 160/100 or above; age 35 or over and smoking 15 or more cigarettes a day.

cards.f: What is the most effective reversible contraceptive?
cards.b: The progestogen-only subdermal implant, which works mainly by inhibiting ovulation. Its failure rate is lower than female sterilisation.

cards.f: Rank emergency contraception options by effectiveness and time window.
cards.b: Copper IUD: most effective, up to 120 hours after the first UPSI or up to 5 days after earliest expected ovulation. Ulipristal acetate: up to 120 hours. Levonorgestrel: licensed up to 72 hours and the least effective.

cards.f: What advice follows ulipristal acetate emergency contraception regarding ongoing hormonal contraception?
cards.b: Wait 5 days before starting or restarting hormonal contraception, because progestogens can reduce ulipristal's effect, and use condoms or abstain meanwhile.

cards.f: How is chlamydia diagnosed and treated?
cards.b: By NAAT on a vulvovaginal swab (women) or first-void urine (men), with other sites tested according to history. First-line treatment is doxycycline, plus partner notification.

cards.f: Why is a test of cure recommended in gonorrhoea?
cards.b: Because of increasing antimicrobial resistance, including to ceftriaxone. Culture before treatment guides sensitivities, and a test of cure confirms eradication.

cards.f: Describe the stages of syphilis.
cards.b: Primary: a painless chancre. Secondary: a widespread rash including the palms and soles, condylomata lata, mucosal lesions and lymphadenopathy. Latent: no symptoms. Tertiary: gummas, cardiovascular disease and neurosyphilis.

cards.f: How do you distinguish bacterial vaginosis from candidiasis?
cards.b: BV gives a thin, grey, fishy-smelling discharge with pH above 4.5 and clue cells, with little itch. Candida gives a thick, curdy, itchy discharge with pH 4.5 or below.

cards.f: What is Gillick competence, and how do the Fraser guidelines relate to it?
cards.b: Gillick competence means a child under 16 has enough maturity and understanding to consent to a particular treatment (Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986]). The Fraser guidelines are the specific criteria for giving contraceptive advice or treatment without parental involvement.

cards.f: What is the time window for HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, and what does U=U mean?
cards.b: PEP should start as soon as possible and within 72 hours of exposure. U=U means a person living with HIV with a sustained undetectable viral load on treatment cannot transmit HIV sexually.

cards.f: Why is partner notification central to STI care?
cards.b: It prevents reinfection of the index patient, finds and treats often-asymptomatic contacts, and interrupts onward transmission.

cards.f: What are the five components of the Apgar score, and when is it recorded?
cards.b: Appearance (colour), pulse, grimace (reflex irritability), activity (tone) and respiration, each scored 0–2. It is recorded at 1, 5 and 10 minutes.

cards.f: In newborn life support, when are chest compressions started, and at what ratio?
cards.b: When the heart rate remains below 60/min despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation. The ratio is 3 compressions to 1 breath.

cards.f: Why are inflation breaths given at the start of newborn resuscitation?
cards.b: To clear lung fluid and aerate the lungs. Most neonatal bradycardia is caused by hypoxia and resolves once the lungs are effectively aerated.

cards.f: Why is jaundice in the first 24 hours of life always pathological?
cards.b: Physiological jaundice does not appear this early. Jaundice under 24 hours suggests haemolysis (rhesus or ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency, spherocytosis) or sepsis, and needs urgent bilirubin measurement.

cards.f: What is prolonged neonatal jaundice, and what must be excluded?
cards.b: Jaundice lasting beyond 14 days in a term baby or 21 days in a preterm baby. Measure conjugated bilirubin to exclude biliary atresia, especially with pale stools and dark urine.

cards.f: Contrast transient tachypnoea of the newborn with respiratory distress syndrome.
cards.b: TTN is caused by delayed clearance of lung fluid, typically in term babies after caesarean birth, and settles within days. RDS is caused by surfactant deficiency in preterm babies, shows ground-glass changes, and is reduced by antenatal corticosteroids and treated with surfactant.

cards.f: What is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis, and what is first-line empirical treatment?
cards.b: Group B streptococcus. First-line treatment is benzylpenicillin with gentamicin, started within an hour of the decision to treat (NICE NG195).

cards.f: List features of necrotising enterocolitis.
cards.b: Usually in preterm babies: feed intolerance, bilious aspirates, abdominal distension, bloody stools and systemic instability. Abdominal X-ray may show pneumatosis intestinalis or free air.

cards.f: What does the newborn and infant physical examination (NIPE) cover?
cards.b: It is done within 72 hours of birth and again at 6–8 weeks. It focuses on the eyes (red reflex), heart, hips and, in boys, testes, alongside a general examination.

cards.f: What does the newborn blood spot test screen for?
cards.b: In England, ten conditions: sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, congenital hypothyroidism, phenylketonuria, MCAD deficiency (MCADD), maple syrup urine disease, isovaleric acidaemia, glutaric aciduria type 1, homocystinuria and (since October 2025) tyrosinaemia type 1. It is ideally taken on day 5.

cards.f: Why is vitamin K given to newborns?
cards.b: Newborns have low vitamin K stores, and breast milk contains little. Vitamin K prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding (haemorrhagic disease of the newborn), which can include intracranial haemorrhage.

cards.f: What are the four developmental domains?
cards.b: Gross motor; fine motor and vision; speech, language and hearing; and social, emotional and behavioural.

cards.f: What is the difference between a median age and a limit age for a milestone?
cards.b: The median age is when half of children achieve the skill. The limit age is when almost all children do, and failure to reach it warrants assessment.

cards.f: By what age should a child walk independently, and what should be checked in a boy who does not?
cards.b: The median is about 12 months and the limit 18 months. In a boy not walking by 18 months, check creatine kinase to screen for Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

cards.f: Why is early hand preference a red flag?
cards.b: Hand preference before about 12 months suggests weakness of the other side, for example hemiplegic cerebral palsy.

cards.f: When should a social smile appear?
cards.b: At about 6 weeks, with a limit of about 8 weeks. Absence suggests visual impairment or a broader developmental or social communication problem.

cards.f: Calculate the corrected age of a baby born at 30 weeks who is now 7 months old.
cards.b: Born 10 weeks early (40 − 30). 10 weeks is about 2.3 months, so the corrected age is 7 − 2.3 ≈ 4.7 months (roughly 4½–5 months). Correction is applied until about 2 years.

cards.f: What should a child be able to copy at 3 and at 4 years?
cards.b: A circle at about 3 years and a cross at about 4 years, with a square and then a triangle following later.

cards.f: What is the first investigation in any child with speech delay?
cards.b: A formal hearing assessment, because hearing loss is a common and treatable cause.

cards.f: Define cerebral palsy.
cards.b: A permanent, non-progressive disorder of movement and posture, caused by a lesion or injury of the developing brain before, during or after birth. The motor picture may change as the child grows.

cards.f: Why does developmental regression need urgent assessment?
cards.b: Loss of acquired skills suggests a progressive process, such as neurodegenerative or metabolic disease, epilepsy syndromes or Rett syndrome. Static causes do not cause regression.

cards.f: What core features define autism?
cards.b: Persistent difficulties in social communication and interaction, and restricted, repetitive patterns of behaviour, interests or activities (including sensory differences), present from early development. NICE CG128 sets out recognition and referral.

cards.f: Give causes of global developmental delay.
cards.b: Genetic (Down syndrome, fragile X, other chromosomal abnormalities), cerebral palsy, congenital infection, metabolic disorders, congenital hypothyroidism, severe neglect, and exposure to alcohol in utero.

cards.f: How does NICE NG143 classify fever in an infant under 3 months?
cards.b: A temperature of 38 °C or higher in an infant under 3 months is a high-risk (red) feature, warranting urgent assessment and usually a septic screen.

cards.f: How does bronchiolitis present, and what is the management?
cards.b: An infant, usually under 1, with coryza progressing to cough, wheeze and crackles, and often poor feeding. Management is supportive (oxygen if hypoxaemic, feeding support), without routine bronchodilators, steroids or antibiotics.

cards.f: Contrast croup with epiglottitis.
cards.b: Croup: a barking cough with stridor in a child who is usually not toxic, often parainfluenza, treated with oral corticosteroid. Epiglottitis: rapid onset, high fever, drooling and tripod posture in a toxic child without a barking cough; do not examine the throat, and secure the airway.

cards.f: Give the biochemical abnormality of pyloric stenosis and why it occurs.
cards.b: Hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, caused by vomiting of gastric acid with renal potassium loss as the kidney conserves sodium.

cards.f: What are the classic features of intussusception?
cards.b: A child aged about 3 months to 2 years with paroxysmal colicky pain, pallor, drawing up the legs, vomiting, redcurrant jelly stool and a sausage-shaped mass. Ultrasound shows a target sign.

cards.f: Why is bilious vomiting in a neonate an emergency?
cards.b: It suggests malrotation with volvulus, which can cause midgut ischaemia within hours. Urgent surgical review and an upper GI contrast study are needed.

cards.f: State the diagnostic criteria for Kawasaki disease.
cards.b: Fever for 5 days or more plus features from: bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis, polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy, oral changes (red cracked lips, strawberry tongue) and changes to the hands and feet. Typically 4 of 5 are needed, but incomplete forms occur.

cards.f: Why is aspirin used in Kawasaki disease despite Reye's syndrome risk?
cards.b: Its anti-inflammatory and antiplatelet effects reduce the risk of coronary artery thrombosis and aneurysm complications. It is used alongside IV immunoglobulin under specialist care.

cards.f: What is the empirical treatment of suspected bacterial meningitis in an infant under 3 months?
cards.b: A third-generation cephalosporin plus amoxicillin, to cover Listeria monocytogenes, which cephalosporins do not cover.

cards.f: Define a simple febrile seizure.
cards.b: A generalised seizure lasting under 15 minutes, not recurring within 24 hours, in a child aged about 6 months to 5 years with fever and no CNS infection.

cards.f: What are life-threatening features of acute asthma in a child?
cards.b: SpO2 below 92%, a silent chest, poor respiratory effort, cyanosis, hypotension, exhaustion and confusion or altered consciousness. In older children, a PEF below 33% of best or predicted.

cards.f: How is clinical dehydration managed in gastroenteritis (NICE CG84)?
cards.b: With oral rehydration solution, given in small frequent amounts, by nasogastric tube if needed. IV fluids are used for shock, or if oral rehydration fails or deterioration occurs.

questions.q: Which screening test is offered at 11+2 to 14+1 weeks to estimate the chance of trisomies 21, 18 and 13?
questions.why: The combined test uses nuchal translucency with PAPP-A and hCG in the dating-scan window. The quadruple test is later and covers trisomy 21 only.

questions.q: A woman has an OGTT at 26 weeks. Which result meets NICE criteria for gestational diabetes?
questions.why: NICE diagnoses GDM with a fasting value of 5.6 mmol/L or more or a 2-hour value of 7.8 mmol/L or more. Only the 2-hour value of 8.1 crosses a threshold.

questions.q: List four blood tests offered at the antenatal booking appointment.
markScheme: Full blood count (anaemia)
Blood group and red cell antibody screen
Infectious disease screening: HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis (any one)
Sickle cell and thalassaemia screening
questions.modelAnswer: At booking, women are offered a full blood count to detect anaemia and a blood group with an antibody screen to identify RhD status and atypical antibodies. Screening for HIV, hepatitis B and syphilis allows interventions to reduce vertical transmission. Sickle cell and thalassaemia screening is offered early, ideally by 10 weeks, so that the partner can be tested and prenatal diagnosis offered in time.

questions.q: Priya Shah, 34, attends booking at 9 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her BMI is 33. Her first baby weighed 4.6 kg, and her mother has type 2 diabetes. She also has chronic hypertension, controlled on medication she started before pregnancy, and her blood group is O RhD-negative. She asks what extra care she will need. Outline the additional risk assessment, screening and management you would plan for her pregnancy.
markScheme: Identifies gestational diabetes risk factors: BMI above 30, previous baby 4.5 kg or more, first-degree relative with diabetes
Arranges OGTT at 24–28 weeks (with early testing considered given multiple risk factors) and explains NICE thresholds
Identifies chronic hypertension as a high risk factor for pre-eclampsia: offer low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks
Reviews antihypertensive: switch away from ACE inhibitors/ARBs if relevant; labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa are used in pregnancy; target BP control
Consultant-led (obstetric) care with more frequent BP and urine monitoring; pre-eclampsia symptom advice
Serial growth scans given hypertension (risk of FGR) and risk of macrosomia
RhD-negative: antibody screen, offer fetal RhD genotyping via cfDNA, routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis if fetus RhD-positive or unknown, anti-D after sensitising events
BMI above 30: higher-dose folic acid advised, VTE risk assessment, anaesthetic review if indicated, vitamin D
Standard screening offered: combined test and anomaly scan, infectious disease and haemoglobinopathy screening
Plans timing and mode of birth discussion; postnatal follow-up of BP and glucose
questions.modelAnswer:
Priya has several risk factors, so she should have consultant-led obstetric care.

Gestational diabetes: her BMI is above 30, her previous baby weighed over 4.5 kg, and her mother has diabetes. Offer an OGTT at 24–28 weeks. With several risk factors, many units would test earlier as well. GDM is diagnosed with a fasting glucose of 5.6 mmol/L or more or a 2-hour value of 7.8 mmol/L or more. Advise on diet and activity now.

Hypertension and pre-eclampsia: chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor for pre-eclampsia, so offer low-dose aspirin from 12 weeks until birth. Review her medication. ACE inhibitors and ARBs should be stopped because of fetal risk, and she can switch to an agent used in pregnancy such as labetalol, nifedipine or methyldopa. Aim for good BP control. She needs more frequent BP and urine checks, baseline renal function, liver tests and platelets, and advice on headache, visual disturbance, epigastric pain and swelling. Hypertension raises the risk of growth restriction, while diabetes risk raises the risk of macrosomia, so plan serial growth scans in the third trimester.

RhD-negative: check the antibody screen at booking and repeat it later in pregnancy. Offer cell-free fetal DNA testing for fetal RhD genotype. If the fetus is RhD-positive or the result is unknown, give routine antenatal anti-D prophylaxis in the third trimester. Give anti-D within 72 hours of any sensitising event, and arrange cord blood testing at birth.

Raised BMI: higher-dose folic acid in the first trimester, vitamin D, VTE risk assessment (she may need thromboprophylaxis depending on overall score), and an anaesthetic review if her BMI warrants it.

Offer routine screening as normal: combined test, anomaly scan, and infectious and haemoglobinopathy screening. Discuss timing and mode of birth later in pregnancy. After birth, she needs BP follow-up, and if she develops GDM, glucose testing to screen for type 2 diabetes.

questions.q: Which CTG feature is considered normal?
options: Variability less than 5 bpm for 60 minutes
Baseline 135 bpm with variability of 10 bpm
questions.why: A normal baseline is 110–160 bpm with variability of 5–25 bpm. The other options are non-reassuring or abnormal features.

questions.q: A primigravida's cervix was 5 cm at 02:00 and is 6 cm at 06:00 with regular contractions and intact membranes. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Offer amniotomy and reassess in 2 hours
Start an oxytocin infusion without further assessment
questions.why: Progress of less than 2 cm in 4 hours raises suspicion of delay. With intact membranes, amniotomy then reassessment after 2 hours is the recommended first step.

questions.q: Name the three Ps that determine the progress of labour, and give one example of a problem with each.
markScheme: Power: uterine contractions, e.g. inefficient or infrequent contractions
Passenger: the fetus, e.g. macrosomia, malposition (occipito-posterior) or malpresentation
Passage: the bony pelvis and soft tissues, e.g. a contracted pelvis or obstructing fibroid
Links poor progress to one or more of these as the basis for assessment
questions.modelAnswer: Progress depends on power, passenger and passage. Power is the strength and frequency of uterine contractions; inefficient contractions are a common cause of delay in first labours. Passenger is the fetus; macrosomia, deflexed occipito-posterior positions or brow presentation slow progress. Passage is the pelvis and soft tissues; a small pelvis or a fibroid in the lower segment can obstruct descent. Assessing delay means assessing each of these.

questions.q: Discuss the indications for continuous CTG monitoring in labour and the limitations of CTG interpretation.
markScheme: Maternal indications: e.g. pre-eclampsia, sepsis or maternal pyrexia, previous caesarean, diabetes, oxytocin use, epidural
Fetal or intrapartum indications: e.g. meconium, fresh bleeding, abnormal intermittent auscultation, suspected growth restriction, prematurity
Limitation: high sensitivity but poor specificity; abnormal traces often occur without acidosis, raising intervention rates
Limitation: inter- and intra-observer variability in interpretation
Interpret in clinical context and by trend, as NICE (2022) emphasises
Fetal blood sampling or escalation/expedited birth used when concerns persist
questions.modelAnswer: Continuous CTG is indicated when maternal or fetal risk factors are present or arise. Maternal examples are pre-eclampsia, sepsis or fever, a uterine scar, diabetes, oxytocin augmentation and epidural analgesia. Fetal and labour examples are significant meconium, fresh bleeding, abnormal intermittent auscultation, suspected growth restriction and prematurity. CTG detects most hypoxic babies but has poor specificity, so many abnormal traces occur in babies without acidosis, and its use has increased operative birth. Interpretation varies between observers. NICE (2022) therefore emphasises the whole clinical picture and trends over time. When concern persists, escalate and consider fetal blood sampling or expedited birth.

questions.q: Emma Clarke, 29, is in her first labour at 40+3 weeks. She was 4 cm at 08:00 and 5 cm at 12:00. Her membranes are intact, contractions are 2 in 10 minutes, and the fetus is cephalic, 2/5 palpable, in an occipito-posterior position. CTG is normal and she is coping with Entonox. Discuss how you would assess and manage her progress.
markScheme: Recognises established first stage with suspected delay: 1 cm in 4 hours (less than 2 cm in 4 hours)
Assesses the three Ps: power (contractions only 2 in 10, suboptimal), passenger (OP position, deflexion, size), passage
Assesses maternal wellbeing: hydration, bladder, pain relief, observations, emotional support
Assesses fetal wellbeing: CTG normal, liquor once membranes ruptured
Offers amniotomy (membranes intact) and reassesses after 2 hours
If progress under 1 cm in 2 hours after amniotomy, diagnoses delay: obstetric review and consider oxytocin
Oxytocin implications: continuous CTG, offer epidural before starting, titrate against contraction frequency, avoid hyperstimulation
Explains how the OP position may rotate with improved contractions; mobilisation/positioning
Discusses escalation if no progress: reassess, consider caesarean for failure to progress or obstruction
Excludes obstruction (caput, moulding, high head) before augmentation
questions.modelAnswer:
Emma is in the established first stage, having been 4 cm at 08:00. She has progressed only 1 cm in 4 hours, which is below the NICE threshold of 2 cm in 4 hours, so delay is suspected.

Assessment should be structured around the three Ps. Power: contractions are only 2 in 10, which suggests inefficient uterine activity, the commonest cause of delay in first labours. Passenger: an occipito-posterior position presents a larger, deflexed diameter and is associated with slower progress and back pain. On examination, record station, caput and moulding; marked caput and moulding with a high head would suggest obstruction. Passage: consider pelvic size, and remember that a full bladder can slow descent.

Also assess Emma herself: observations, hydration, bladder emptying, pain and her wishes, offering an epidural if she wants one. Assess the fetus: the CTG is currently normal.

Management: explain the findings and offer amniotomy, which can strengthen contractions and lets you see the liquor. Reassess with a vaginal examination after 2 hours. If progress is still less than 1 cm, delay is confirmed and she needs obstetric review. Exclude obstruction before considering an oxytocin infusion. Oxytocin needs continuous CTG, and an epidural should be offered before starting, because contractions become more painful. Titrate to about 4–5 contractions in 10 minutes and avoid hyperstimulation, which compromises fetal oxygenation. Reassess after a further period. Better contractions often rotate an OP head to OA. Upright positions and mobilisation may help.

If progress fails despite adequate contractions, or signs of obstruction or fetal compromise develop, recommend caesarean birth. Throughout, keep Emma informed, support her choices, record findings on the partogram and maintain continuity of midwifery care.

questions.q: What is the most common cause of primary postpartum haemorrhage?
questions.why: Tone (uterine atony) accounts for most primary PPH, which is why uterine massage and uterotonics are first-line.

questions.q: During PPH from atony in a woman with severe asthma who has already received oxytocin and ergometrine, which uterotonic should be avoided?
questions.why: Carboprost is a prostaglandin F2α analogue that can cause bronchospasm, so it is relatively contraindicated in asthma. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic, not a uterotonic.

questions.q: Describe how magnesium sulfate toxicity is monitored and managed.
markScheme: Monitor deep tendon reflexes (lost first)
Monitor respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and urine output (reduced output means accumulation, as magnesium is renally excreted)
Stop the infusion and give calcium gluconate if toxicity occurs
questions.modelAnswer: Magnesium is renally cleared, so toxicity is more likely with oliguria, which is common in severe pre-eclampsia. Check deep tendon reflexes regularly, because their loss is an early sign. Monitor respiratory rate and oxygen saturation for respiratory depression, and record hourly urine output. If toxicity is suspected, stop the infusion, support breathing and give calcium gluconate as the antidote.

questions.q: Outline the immediate management of suspected umbilical cord prolapse at 38 weeks in a woman whose cervix is 5 cm dilated.
markScheme: Call for help and declare an obstetric emergency
Relieve cord compression by manually elevating the presenting part or filling the bladder
Position the woman knee–chest or head-down left lateral
Minimise handling of the cord (to avoid vasospasm), keep it moist and warm if outside the vagina
Arrange Category 1 caesarean section, with neonatal team present
questions.modelAnswer: Call for help immediately: a senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, midwives and the neonatal team. Relieve pressure on the cord by pushing the presenting part up digitally or by filling the bladder with saline through a catheter. Place the woman knee–chest or head-down in the left lateral position. Avoid handling the cord, which can cause vasospasm. At 5 cm, vaginal birth is not imminent, so arrange a Category 1 caesarean and continue fetal monitoring.

questions.q: Aisha Begum, 31, has a vaginal birth of a 4.1 kg baby after a 14-hour labour augmented with oxytocin. Ten minutes after delivery of the placenta, the midwife reports heavy bleeding with an estimated loss of 1200 ml. Aisha is pale, her heart rate is 124/min and her BP is 96/58. The uterus is soft and boggy above the umbilicus. Describe your management.
markScheme: Recognises major primary PPH (more than 1000 ml with signs of shock); likely atony given risk factors (macrosomia, prolonged augmented labour)
Calls for help: senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, midwife coordinator, haematology/blood bank, activates major haemorrhage protocol
ABC: high-flow oxygen, lie flat, two large-bore cannulae
Bloods: FBC, coagulation including fibrinogen, crossmatch, U&E, lactate/venous gas
Warmed crystalloid then blood and blood products early (O-negative or group-specific), guided by clinical picture and coagulation
Mechanical: uterine massage to rub up a contraction, bimanual compression, catheterise to empty bladder
Pharmacological: oxytocin, ergometrine (if not hypertensive), carboprost (if not asthmatic), misoprostol; tranexamic acid
Checks placenta and membranes complete; examines for trauma (other Ts); considers thrombin
Escalation to theatre: examination under anaesthesia, intrauterine balloon tamponade, B-Lynch suture, uterine artery ligation, interventional radiology, hysterectomy as last resort
Monitoring: continuous observations, catheter with hourly urine output, accurate blood loss by weighing, scribe and documentation
Aftercare: HDU, VTE prophylaxis once bleeding controlled, debrief, incident reporting
questions.modelAnswer:
Aisha has a major primary PPH: over 1000 ml lost, with tachycardia and borderline hypotension showing shock. A soft, boggy uterus after a macrosomic baby and a long oxytocin-augmented labour points to atony.

Call for help immediately: the senior obstetrician, anaesthetist, additional midwives and porters. Activate the major haemorrhage protocol and alert the blood bank. Assign a scribe to record times, interventions and cumulative loss.

Resuscitation runs alongside stopping the bleeding. Give high-flow oxygen, lie her flat, and insert two large-bore cannulae. Send blood for FBC, coagulation screen including fibrinogen, crossmatch, renal function and a venous gas with lactate. Give warmed crystalloid initially, but move early to red cells, using O-negative or group-specific blood if needed. Give plasma and other products guided by coagulation results and ongoing loss. Monitor observations continuously, insert a catheter for hourly urine output, and weigh swabs and drapes to measure loss.

To treat atony, rub up a contraction with fundal massage and keep the bladder empty. Apply bimanual compression if bleeding continues. Give uterotonics in sequence: an oxytocin bolus and infusion, ergometrine if she is not hypertensive, carboprost if she does not have asthma, and misoprostol. Give tranexamic acid.

Check the other Ts. Inspect the placenta and membranes for completeness, and examine for cervical, vaginal and perineal tears. Look for coagulopathy, including clotting results and oozing from cannula sites.

If bleeding continues despite medical measures, transfer to theatre for examination under anaesthesia. Options there include an intrauterine balloon tamponade, then compression sutures such as a B-Lynch, uterine artery ligation or interventional radiology embolisation if available. Hysterectomy is the last resort and should be decided early enough to save her life.

Afterwards she needs high-dependency care, haemoglobin and coagulation monitoring, and VTE prophylaxis once haemostasis is secure, because PPH and transfusion raise thrombotic risk. Give her and her partner a debrief, and complete incident reporting.

questions.q: Discuss the following proposition: "The safest response to shoulder dystocia is speed: the faster the baby is delivered, the better the outcome." Use the pathophysiology, recognised risk factors and evidence-based manoeuvres to support your answer.
markScheme: Defines shoulder dystocia: the need for additional obstetric manoeuvres after gentle traction fails, due to impaction of the anterior shoulder behind the symphysis (rarely posterior on the sacral promontory)
Pathophysiology of hypoxia: cord compression and impaired venous return; the risk of hypoxic injury rises with head-to-body interval, so timeliness matters
Counterpoint: excessive or rushed traction, especially lateral/downward traction, causes brachial plexus injury; speed must not mean force
Risk factors: macrosomia, maternal diabetes, previous shoulder dystocia, high BMI, prolonged or augmented labour, assisted vaginal birth, but most cases are unpredictable
Structured approach: call for help, stop pushing, avoid fundal pressure, McRoberts and suprapubic pressure first (resolves many cases)
Internal manoeuvres: delivery of posterior arm or rotational manoeuvres; consider episiotomy for access, not as a stand-alone manoeuvre; all-fours position
Third-line options: cleidotomy, symphysiotomy, Zavanelli manoeuvre as last resort
Neonatal team present; post-delivery assessment for brachial plexus injury, clavicle/humerus fracture, hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy
Maternal complications: PPH, third- and fourth-degree tears
Role of drills/simulation training and documentation (timings, which shoulder anterior, manoeuvres, personnel)
Balanced conclusion: timely, calm, systematic manoeuvres rather than speed alone or forceful traction
questions.modelAnswer:
Shoulder dystocia is a vaginal cephalic birth where extra manoeuvres are needed after gentle traction fails to deliver the shoulders. Usually the anterior shoulder impacts behind the pubic symphysis.

The proposition is partly right. Once the head is born, the cord is compressed between the fetal body and the pelvis, and venous congestion of the head and neck impairs perfusion. The risk of hypoxic-ischaemic injury and death rises as the head-to-body interval lengthens, so delay is dangerous. A prompt, organised response matters.

However, speed pursued through force is harmful. Strong or lateral traction on the head stretches the upper brachial plexus and causes Erb's palsy, which can be permanent. Fundal pressure worsens impaction and is associated with uterine rupture. Panic leads to uncoordinated, repeated traction. The goal is therefore efficient, systematic manoeuvres, not haste for its own sake.

Risk factors include fetal macrosomia, maternal diabetes, previous shoulder dystocia, high maternal BMI, prolonged or augmented labour, and assisted vaginal birth. Most cases occur without risk factors and cannot be predicted, so every team must be ready for it.

The structured response begins with calling for help, including the neonatal team, and stopping maternal pushing. McRoberts' position flattens the lumbosacral angle and rotates the symphysis upwards. Suprapubic pressure from behind the anterior shoulder adducts and rotates it. These simple steps resolve a large proportion of cases. If they fail, internal manoeuvres follow: delivering the posterior arm reduces the shoulder diameter, and rotational manoeuvres move the shoulders into an oblique diameter. An episiotomy may improve access but does not itself relieve bony impaction. The all-fours position is an alternative. Rare last-resort procedures such as cleidotomy, symphysiotomy or cephalic replacement have been described.

After birth, the baby needs assessment for brachial plexus injury, fractures and encephalopathy. The mother needs assessment for PPH and anal sphincter injury. Documentation should record the timings, which shoulder was anterior, the manoeuvres used and who was present. Regular multiprofessional drills improve outcomes.

In conclusion, outcome depends on timeliness combined with correct technique. A calm, rehearsed, stepwise approach is safest; speed alone, especially through excessive traction, is not.

questions.q: A 61-year-old woman has postmenopausal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. What is the next step?
questions.why: An endometrial thickness of 4 mm or more in postmenopausal bleeding needs histological assessment to exclude hyperplasia or carcinoma.

questions.q: A 27-year-old has irregular cycles, acne and hirsutism. Explain how PCOS is diagnosed.
markScheme: Rotterdam criteria: two of three features required
Oligo- or anovulation; clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (e.g. raised free androgen index); polycystic ovarian morphology on ultrasound (or raised AMH in adults under the 2023 guideline)
Exclude other causes: thyroid disease, hyperprolactinaemia, non-classical CAH, and androgen-secreting tumours if severe or rapid virilisation
Notes that she already has two criteria clinically (irregular cycles and hirsutism or acne)
questions.modelAnswer: PCOS is diagnosed with the Rotterdam criteria, which need two of three: oligo- or anovulation, clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism, and polycystic ovarian morphology (or raised AMH in adults under the 2023 international guideline). She already meets two criteria clinically, so imaging is not needed for diagnosis. Exclude mimics with TSH, prolactin and 17-hydroxyprogesterone, and test testosterone. A very high level or rapid virilisation suggests an androgen-secreting tumour.

questions.q: Hannah Lewis, 26, presents to the emergency department with left iliac fossa pain and light vaginal bleeding. Her last menstrual period was 7 weeks ago and her urine pregnancy test is positive. Her pulse is 92/min, BP 118/74, and she has left adnexal tenderness without peritonism. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus and a 2.5 cm left adnexal mass with no fetal heartbeat. Serum hCG is 1,400 IU/L. Discuss your diagnosis and the management options.
markScheme: Diagnosis: likely left tubal ectopic pregnancy (empty uterus, adnexal mass, positive test), haemodynamically stable
Differentials: pregnancy of unknown location, early intrauterine pregnancy/miscarriage, corpus luteum cyst, appendicitis
Initial: assess for rupture/haemorrhage, IV access, FBC, group and save, rhesus status; senior gynaecology review

Expectant management: only if stable, pain-free, unruptured mass under 35 mm without heartbeat; NICE offers it at hCG 1,000 IU/L or less and says consider it at 1,000–1,500; serial hCG with clear safety-netting

Medical management with methotrexate (folate antagonist): criteria include no significant pain, unruptured mass under 35 mm, no heartbeat, hCG below 1,500 (offered up to 5,000 with choice); requires follow-up hCG and reliable attendance

Methotrexate counselling: avoid pregnancy for a period after treatment, side effects, possible need for further dose or surgery, avoid folate-containing supplements temporarily, contraindications (e.g. liver/renal disease, breastfeeding, intrauterine pregnancy)

Surgical management: laparoscopic salpingectomy if contralateral tube healthy, or salpingotomy if fertility risk factors; indicated if pain, rupture, mass 35 mm or more, heartbeat or hCG 5,000 or more
Anti-D for RhD-negative women undergoing surgical management
Recognises that with hCG 1,400, a 25 mm mass and no heartbeat, methotrexate is first-line if pain is not significant; expectant management requires her to be pain-free; shared decision-making
Psychological support, follow-up, future pregnancy advice (early scan due to recurrence risk)
questions.modelAnswer:
Hannah has a positive pregnancy test, pain, bleeding, an empty uterus and a left adnexal mass. This is most likely a left tubal ectopic pregnancy. She is haemodynamically stable with no peritonism, which suggests it has not ruptured. Differentials include pregnancy of unknown location, early miscarriage, a corpus luteum cyst and appendicitis, but the ultrasound findings strongly favour ectopic pregnancy.

Initial care: obtain senior gynaecology review, IV access, FBC, blood group and save, and rhesus status. Reassess regularly, because rupture can cause sudden haemorrhage.

NICE NG126 describes three options.

Expectant management may be offered to a woman who is clinically stable and pain-free, with an unruptured tubal mass under 35 mm, no heartbeat and an hCG of 1,000 IU/L or less. NICE says it should also be considered when the hCG is above 1,000 but below 1,500 IU/L and the other criteria are met. It needs serial hCG monitoring and clear advice to return urgently with worsening pain, dizziness or shoulder-tip pain.

Medical management with methotrexate, a folate antagonist that stops trophoblast proliferation, is first-line under similar criteria: no significant pain, an unruptured mass under 35 mm with no heartbeat, an hCG below 1,500 IU/L, and no intrauterine pregnancy. It can be offered as a choice up to 5,000 IU/L. It requires reliable follow-up with serial hCG, and sometimes a further dose or surgery. Counsel her about side effects, the need to avoid pregnancy for some months afterwards, and temporarily avoiding folate supplements. Contraindications include significant hepatic or renal disease and breastfeeding.

Surgical management is required with significant pain, a mass of 35 mm or more, a fetal heartbeat, an hCG of 5,000 IU/L or more, or signs of rupture. Laparoscopic salpingectomy is preferred if the other tube is healthy. Salpingotomy may be considered with contralateral tubal disease, but it needs hCG follow-up for persistent trophoblast. RhD-negative women having surgery should receive anti-D.

With an hCG of 1,400 IU/L, a 2.5 cm mass, no heartbeat and mild pain, Hannah meets the criteria for first-line methotrexate if her pain is not significant, and surgery remains an alternative. Expectant management is less suitable because she is not pain-free, although her hCG is in the range where NICE says it can be considered. The choice follows shared decision-making, guided by her preferences and ability to attend follow-up. She should also be offered psychological support, signposting, and an early scan in any future pregnancy, because her recurrence risk is higher.

questions.q: Margaret Hughes, 63, is referred by her GP with 4 months of abdominal bloating, early satiety and urinary frequency. She went through the menopause at 51. Serum CA-125 is 180 U/mL. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 9 cm right adnexal mass that is multilocular, with solid areas and a small amount of ascites. Calculate her Risk of Malignancy Index, and discuss its interpretation and the further management of her case.
markScheme: Recognises NICE red-flag symptoms of ovarian cancer (persistent bloating, early satiety, urinary frequency) in a postmenopausal woman, warranting CA-125 then ultrasound
Defines RMI = U × M × CA-125
Ultrasound score: features include multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites, metastases; 2 or more features gives U = 3 (one feature U = 1, none U = 0)
Postmenopausal so M = 3
Calculates RMI = 3 × 3 × 180 = 1620
Interprets: RMI of 250 or more indicates high risk and warrants referral to a specialist gynaecological oncology MDT (NICE)
Further imaging: CT of abdomen and pelvis (staging), consider chest imaging; tumour markers and baseline bloods
Ascitic sampling or image-guided biopsy for histology if primary surgery not appropriate; avoid cyst rupture/aspiration of a suspicious mass
Management outline: MDT-led, usually cytoreductive surgery aiming for no residual disease plus platinum-based chemotherapy (neoadjuvant or adjuvant)
Notes CA-125 limitations and differentials (benign tumours, endometriosis less likely postmenopausally, other cancers such as GI metastasis)
Considers germline BRCA testing and genetic counselling given implications for treatment (PARP inhibitors) and family
Holistic care: clinical nurse specialist, breaking bad news, consent and shared decisions
questions.modelAnswer:
Margaret has persistent bloating, early satiety and urinary frequency. In a postmenopausal woman, NICE treats these as possible ovarian cancer and advises CA-125 first, then pelvic ultrasound if it is raised. Both are abnormal here.

The Risk of Malignancy Index (RMI) is U × M × CA-125.

- U is the ultrasound score. Each of these features counts: multilocular cyst, solid areas, bilateral lesions, ascites and intra-abdominal metastases. No features gives U = 0, one gives U = 1, and two or more give U = 3. Margaret has a multilocular cyst, solid areas and ascites, so U = 3.
- M is the menopausal status score: 3 if postmenopausal and 1 if premenopausal. She is postmenopausal, so M = 3.
- Her CA-125 is 180 U/mL.
