RMI = 3 × 3 × 180 = 1620.

NICE uses an RMI of 250 or more as the threshold for referral to a specialist gynaecological oncology multidisciplinary team. Her score is far above this, so malignancy is highly likely. RMI is a triage tool, not a diagnosis. CA-125 can be raised by benign conditions and other cancers, and early-stage tumours may not raise it.

Refer urgently under the suspected cancer pathway. Stage the disease with CT of the abdomen and pelvis, plus chest imaging. Take baseline bloods, and consider other tumour markers to exclude a gastrointestinal primary metastasising to the ovary. Do not aspirate a suspicious mass, because rupture can upstage disease. If primary surgery is unsuitable, histology can be obtained by image-guided biopsy or ascitic cytology.

The MDT will plan treatment. This is usually cytoreductive surgery aiming for no visible residual disease, combined with platinum-based chemotherapy. Chemotherapy may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) when complete resection is unlikely initially. Offer germline BRCA testing with genetic counselling, because the result guides maintenance therapy, such as PARP inhibitors, and has implications for relatives.

She should be told the findings sensitively, supported by a clinical nurse specialist, and involved in shared decisions about her treatment.

questions.q: Which is the most effective method of emergency contraception?
options: Combined oral contraceptive taken in double quantity
questions.why: The copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception and also provides ongoing contraception.

questions.q: A 34-year-old who smokes 20 cigarettes a day requests the combined pill. Her BP is 128/80 and she has migraine without aura. Which statement is correct under UKMEC?
options: Her migraine without aura makes the COC UKMEC 4
Smoking makes the COC UKMEC 4 at her current age
The COC is UKMEC 3 for her because she is under 35 and smokes
Her age and smoking make the COC UKMEC 2
questions.why: Under UKMEC, smoking in a woman under 35 is category 2 for combined methods. The category rises to 3 or 4 from age 35, depending on how much she smokes. Migraine without aura is not category 4 either; aura is the key feature.

questions.q: Give two mechanisms by which the levonorgestrel intrauterine system prevents pregnancy.
markScheme: Thickens cervical mucus, impeding sperm penetration
Thins (suppresses) the endometrium, preventing implantation; ovulation is inhibited in some cycles
questions.modelAnswer: The levonorgestrel IUS releases progestogen locally. This thickens cervical mucus, which stops sperm entering the upper genital tract. It also suppresses endometrial proliferation, making the endometrium thin and unreceptive. Ovulation continues in most users, although it is suppressed in some cycles.

questions.q: A 19-year-old has a vaginal discharge. Compare bacterial vaginosis and trichomoniasis in terms of transmission, features, investigation and treatment class.
markScheme: BV is not sexually transmitted (associated with sexual activity); trichomoniasis is an STI requiring partner treatment
BV: thin grey fishy discharge, pH above 4.5, clue cells (Amsel criteria/Gram stain)
Trichomoniasis: frothy yellow-green discharge, vulvitis, strawberry cervix; diagnosed by NAAT or microscopy
Both treated with a nitroimidazole (metronidazole)
questions.modelAnswer: Bacterial vaginosis is an overgrowth of anaerobes replacing lactobacilli. It is associated with, but not caused by, sexual activity, so partners are not routinely treated. It causes a thin, grey, fishy discharge with pH above 4.5, and clue cells are seen. Trichomonas vaginalis is a sexually transmitted protozoan causing frothy yellow-green discharge, vulvitis and sometimes a strawberry cervix; it is diagnosed by NAAT. Both are treated with metronidazole, and trichomoniasis also needs partner notification and STI screening.

questions.q: Jade Morris, 17, attends a sexual health clinic requesting emergency contraception. She had unprotected sex 80 hours ago with a new partner, and she is on day 14 of a regular 28-day cycle. She has no medical conditions, takes no regular medication and has never used contraception before. She is anxious about having an intrauterine device fitted. She mentions a slight vaginal discharge, and she wants to start a reliable ongoing method. Outline your management.
markScheme: Confidential consultation; assess Gillick/competence (she is 17, so presumed competent at 16+, but safeguarding still considered: age and relationship of partner, coercion, CSE risk factors)
Emergency contraception options explained: copper IUD most effective, can be fitted (within 120 hours of UPSI)
Ulipristal acetate valid within 120 hours; levonorgestrel licensed only to 72 hours so not appropriate at 80 hours
Mid-cycle timing (around ovulation) increases pregnancy risk and favours Cu-IUD
Interactions: check enzyme inducers, BMI considerations; vomiting advice
Ongoing contraception: Cu-IUD continues as contraception; if ulipristal used, wait 5 days before starting hormonal method, use condoms, quick start thereafter
LARC discussed: implant, IUS, as most effective
Pregnancy test 3 weeks after UPSI (or if period late/abnormal)
STI screening: chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV and syphilis serology (window periods explained), consider swabs for discharge; offer treatment as indicated
Condom use and partner notification; consider HIV PEP not indicated unless high-risk exposure
questions.modelAnswer:
Start with a confidential, non-judgemental consultation. At 17, Jade is presumed to have capacity to consent. Still explore safeguarding: the partner's age, whether the sex was consensual, and any coercion, exploitation, alcohol or drug factors.

Emergency contraception: she is 80 hours after unprotected sex and around the time of ovulation on day 14, so her pregnancy risk is relatively high. The copper IUD is the most effective option and can be fitted up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse. It works regardless of ovulation and also provides immediate, long-term contraception. Levonorgestrel is licensed only up to 72 hours, so it is not appropriate now. Ulipristal acetate can be used up to 120 hours, but oral methods are less effective once ovulation has occurred. Offer the copper IUD first. If she declines or fitting is unavailable, give ulipristal. Check for enzyme-inducing drugs and give advice on vomiting.

Ongoing contraception: if she has the copper IUD, it can stay as her method. If she takes ulipristal, she should wait 5 days before starting hormonal contraception, because progestogens can reduce its effect. She can then quick-start a method such as the implant, IUS or pill, using condoms or abstaining until it is effective. Discuss LARC as the most effective option, and note that an IUS can later replace a copper IUD.

Follow-up: she should have a pregnancy test 3 weeks after this episode, or sooner if her period is late or unusual.

STI care: a new partner and a discharge mean she needs screening. Test for chlamydia and gonorrhoea by NAAT, take swabs as indicated for the discharge, and offer HIV and syphilis blood tests, explaining window periods and repeat testing. If an IUD is fitted, current guidance allows same-day fitting with STI testing and treatment if positive, unless there are signs of pelvic infection. Advise condom use, discuss partner notification if a test is positive, and provide written information and safety-netting.

questions.q: In newborn life support, at what heart rate are chest compressions started after effective ventilation?
questions.why: Compressions start if the heart rate stays below 60/min despite effective ventilation, at a 3:1 ratio with breaths.

questions.q: List four causes of jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life.
markScheme: Rhesus haemolytic disease
ABO incompatibility
G6PD deficiency or hereditary spherocytosis
Congenital infection or sepsis
questions.modelAnswer: Jaundice in the first day is pathological. The main cause is haemolysis: rhesus disease, ABO incompatibility (often a group O mother with a group A or B baby), and red cell defects such as G6PD deficiency or hereditary spherocytosis. Sepsis and congenital infection are other important causes. Investigate urgently with serum bilirubin, blood group, a direct antiglobulin test and a full blood count.

questions.q: Baby Lily, a term breastfed infant, is reviewed at 17 days old because she is still jaundiced. Her mother says Lily is feeding well, but her stools have become pale and her urine is dark yellow. She was born at 39 weeks after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and her newborn examination was normal. Her weight is just above birth weight. Discuss your assessment and the key diagnosis to exclude.
markScheme: Defines prolonged jaundice: beyond 14 days in a term baby
Key concern: conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, particularly biliary atresia, given pale stools and dark urine
History: feeding, stool colour (use stool chart), urine, weight, family history, maternal blood group, prenatal scans, symptoms of hypothyroidism or infection
Examination: hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, dysmorphism, signs of infection, bruising (vitamin K deficiency bleeding risk)
Investigations: total and conjugated bilirubin (conjugated above about 25 µmol/L is significant), LFTs, FBC, blood group and DAT, thyroid function, urine culture
Check newborn blood spot result (congenital hypothyroidism)
Urgent referral to paediatric liver unit for biliary atresia assessment: ultrasound, further tests
Explains time-critical Kasai portoenterostomy: better outcomes if done early; may later need liver transplant
Contrasts with breast milk jaundice (unconjugated, normal stool and urine, well baby)
Gives vitamin K consideration given risk of fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
questions.modelAnswer:
Lily has prolonged jaundice, meaning jaundice beyond 14 days in a term baby. Breast milk jaundice is common at this age, but it is unconjugated, and the baby is well with normal yellow stools. Lily's pale stools and dark urine instead suggest conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with cholestasis. Biliary atresia must be excluded urgently.

History: ask about feeding, weight gain, stool colour (using a stool colour chart), urine colour, vomiting, lethargy and bleeding or bruising. Also ask about the pregnancy and antenatal scans, maternal blood group, family history of liver or metabolic disease, and features of hypothyroidism.

Examination: look for hepatomegaly or splenomegaly, dysmorphic features (for example Alagille syndrome), cardiac murmurs, signs of infection, and bruising. Cholestasis impairs vitamin K absorption, so there is a risk of serious bleeding.

Investigations: measure total and conjugated bilirubin. A conjugated level above about 25 µmol/L is significant and needs urgent investigation. Also send liver function tests and clotting, FBC, blood group with a direct antiglobulin test, thyroid function (and confirm the newborn blood spot result), and urine culture to exclude infection.

Management: with conjugated jaundice and pale stools, refer urgently to a specialist paediatric liver unit. Ultrasound and further tests there will evaluate biliary atresia and other causes, such as metabolic disease, infection and genetic cholestatic syndromes. Biliary atresia is a progressive obliteration of the bile ducts. Outcomes after Kasai portoenterostomy are better the earlier it is done, ideally within the first weeks of life, and some children later need liver transplantation. Give vitamin K as advised by specialists, because of malabsorption.

In summary, prolonged jaundice with pale stools is never put down to breastfeeding without a normal conjugated bilirubin.

questions.q: Baby Oliver is born at 35+2 weeks after spontaneous rupture of membranes 26 hours before birth. His mother had a temperature of 38.4 °C in labour and is known to carry group B streptococcus; she did not receive intrapartum antibiotics. At 6 hours old, Oliver is grunting, his respiratory rate is 72/min, his temperature is 35.9 °C and he is feeding poorly. Describe your assessment and management.
markScheme: Recognises high risk of early-onset neonatal sepsis: maternal GBS, prolonged rupture, maternal intrapartum fever, preterm, no intrapartum antibiotics, and clinical signs (respiratory distress, temperature instability, poor feeding)
Uses NICE NG195 approach: red flag or multiple risk factors means start antibiotics without delay (within 1 hour)
ABC assessment: oxygen saturations, respiratory support as needed, heart rate, capillary refill, glucose
Differentials of respiratory distress: sepsis/pneumonia, TTN, RDS (late preterm), pneumothorax, congenital heart disease
Investigations: blood culture before antibiotics, CRP (at presentation and 18–24 hours), FBC, blood gas, glucose, chest X-ray
Lumbar puncture if strong suspicion or positive culture, or clinical meningitis signs, when stable
First-line empirical antibiotics: benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin intravenously, with gentamicin level monitoring
Supportive care: thermal care, fluids/glucose, feeding support (IV or NG), admission to neonatal unit
Review at 36 hours: stop antibiotics if cultures negative, CRP reassuring and baby well; continue if confirmed infection (course length per site, longer for meningitis)
Communication with parents, and informing obstetric team; advise mother about GBS in future pregnancies (intrapartum antibiotics offered)
questions.modelAnswer:
Oliver is at very high risk of early-onset neonatal infection. His risk factors are maternal GBS carriage without intrapartum antibiotics, rupture of membranes for over 24 hours, maternal fever in labour and late prematurity. He also has clinical signs: respiratory distress, hypothermia and poor feeding. Under NICE NG195, these features mean starting antibiotics without waiting for results, ideally within an hour.

Assessment begins with ABC. Measure oxygen saturations and give oxygen or non-invasive respiratory support as needed. Assess heart rate, capillary refill time and blood pressure. Check blood glucose, because septic and preterm babies can become hypoglycaemic. Consider other causes of respiratory distress alongside sepsis: transient tachypnoea, respiratory distress syndrome in a late preterm baby, pneumothorax and congenital heart disease.

Investigations: take a blood culture before the first antibiotic dose. Also send a CRP (repeated at about 18–24 hours), FBC, blood gas with lactate and glucose, and arrange a chest X-ray. Do a lumbar puncture when he is stable if there is strong clinical suspicion, neurological signs, a positive blood culture or a markedly raised CRP.

Give the first-line empirical regimen of intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin. Monitor gentamicin levels because of its renal and ototoxic effects. Admit him to the neonatal unit for thermal care and incubator warming. Give IV fluids or glucose while feeding is poor, and introduce NG feeds when appropriate. Monitor him continuously.

At around 36 hours, review the case. If the blood culture is negative, the CRP values are reassuring and he is clinically well, stop antibiotics. If infection is confirmed, continue treatment for a course appropriate to the site, which is longer for meningitis, and seek microbiology advice.

Communicate clearly with the parents throughout. Inform the obstetric team. Advise the mother that, because she carries GBS, she should be offered intrapartum antibiotics in future labours. Any GBS infection should be documented in the baby's records.

questions.q: By what age should almost all children be walking independently (the limit age)?
questions.why: The median age for walking is about 12 months, and the limit is 18 months. Boys not walking by then should have creatine kinase checked.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy has no words, poor eye contact and lines up his toys. His parents report he had a few words at 15 months that he has since lost. Outline your initial approach.
markScheme: Recognises regression of language as a red flag needing prompt assessment
Formal audiology to exclude hearing loss
Consider autism (social communication difficulty plus restricted, repetitive behaviour) and refer to specialist autism assessment
Full history and examination including growth, head circumference, neurocutaneous stigmata and dysmorphism; consider Landau–Kleffner/epileptic causes
Consider genetic testing such as fragile X and microarray, and refer to a child development team
questions.modelAnswer: Loss of words he previously had is regression, so he needs prompt assessment rather than reassurance. Arrange formal audiology first. His poor eye contact and repetitive play suggest autism, so refer him to a specialist autism team as NICE recommends. A full history and examination should include head circumference, skin examination for neurocutaneous signs, and dysmorphism. Consider an EEG if seizures or an epileptic aphasia are suspected. Genetic testing (fragile X, microarray) and child development team input are appropriate.

questions.q: Sami, a boy now 20 months old, is brought by his parents because he is not yet walking. He was born at term. He sat at 9 months and is now able to pull to stand. He says about 10 words, uses a pincer grip and enjoys interactive games. His maternal uncle used a wheelchair from adolescence. Discuss your assessment and investigation.
markScheme: Recognises isolated gross motor delay: not walking beyond the 18-month limit, with other domains broadly normal
Notes term birth so no correction needed
Family history in maternal uncle suggests X-linked condition: Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophy
History: pregnancy, birth, milestones, regression, falls, toe walking, difficulty climbing, family pedigree
Examination: Gowers' sign, calf pseudohypertrophy, tone, power, reflexes, hip examination, spine, dysmorphism, growth
Differentials: Duchenne/Becker, cerebral palsy (e.g. spastic diplegia), spinal muscular atrophy, developmental dysplasia of the hip, benign hypotonia/bottom shuffler, global delay
Key investigation: serum creatine kinase (markedly raised in Duchenne)
Genetic testing of dystrophin gene; muscle biopsy now rarely needed
Other tests guided by findings: thyroid, hip imaging, MRI brain if upper motor neurone signs
Refer to paediatric neurology and physiotherapy; genetic counselling for family (maternal carrier testing)
questions.modelAnswer:
Sami is 20 months old, born at term so no correction is needed, and not yet walking. This is past the 18-month limit age. His language, fine motor and social skills are broadly age-appropriate, so this is isolated gross motor delay. The history of a maternal uncle who needed a wheelchair from adolescence suggests an X-linked neuromuscular disorder, especially Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy.

History: confirm his milestones and check for regression. Ask about falls, toe walking, difficulty rising from the floor and fatigue. Take a full pregnancy and birth history, and draw a three-generation pedigree, focusing on maternal male relatives and any cardiac disease.

Examination: watch him rise from the floor for Gowers' sign, where he climbs up his legs with his hands. Look for calf pseudohypertrophy. Assess tone, power and reflexes: upper motor neurone signs would point towards cerebral palsy, while hypotonia with absent reflexes suggests spinal muscular atrophy. Examine the hips for developmental dysplasia and the spine for dysraphism, and check growth, head circumference and dysmorphism.

Differentials: Duchenne or Becker muscular dystrophy; cerebral palsy, such as spastic diplegia; spinal muscular atrophy; developmental hip dysplasia; benign hypotonia, or a bottom-shuffling pattern, which often runs in families; and evolving global delay.

Investigations: the key first test is serum creatine kinase, which is markedly raised in Duchenne. If it is raised, confirm with genetic testing of the dystrophin gene; muscle biopsy is now rarely needed. Further tests depend on the findings: thyroid function, hip ultrasound or X-ray, and brain MRI if there are upper motor neurone signs.

Refer to paediatric neurology and physiotherapy. If Duchenne is confirmed, he needs multidisciplinary care, including cardiac and respiratory surveillance, and the family need genetic counselling with carrier testing for his mother and female relatives.

questions.q: A 5-week-old boy has projectile non-bilious vomiting after every feed and is hungry afterwards. Which blood gas is most likely?
questions.why: Loss of gastric acid in pyloric stenosis causes hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, with hypokalaemia from renal potassium loss.

questions.q: Describe the features and initial management of croup in an 18-month-old.
markScheme: Viral (usually parainfluenza), 6 months–3 years, coryzal prodrome
Barking cough, hoarse voice, inspiratory stridor, worse at night
Single dose of oral corticosteroid for all severities; minimal handling to avoid distress
Severe or worsening: oxygen and nebulised adrenaline as a bridge, with senior and anaesthetic involvement
questions.modelAnswer: Croup is a viral laryngotracheobronchitis, usually caused by parainfluenza, in children aged 6 months to 3 years. After a coryzal prodrome, a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor develop, often worse at night. All severities are treated with a single dose of oral corticosteroid, and the child is kept calm with a parent. Stridor at rest, recession or agitation suggests severe disease: give oxygen and nebulised adrenaline for temporary relief, and involve senior and anaesthetic colleagues.

questions.modelAnswer:
Leo has had fever for more than 5 days with all five principal features: bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection, oral changes, a polymorphous rash, cervical lymphadenopathy and changes in the hands and feet. With a markedly raised CRP, the most likely diagnosis is Kawasaki disease, a medium-vessel vasculitis of unknown cause that mostly affects young children.

Differentials include scarlet fever, measles, adenovirus infection, toxic shock syndrome, PIMS-TS (MIS-C), drug reactions and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Kawasaki disease must be recognised promptly because of its cardiac complications.

The major complication is coronary artery aneurysm, a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in high-income countries. Early treatment greatly reduces this risk. Other cardiac complications include myocarditis, pericarditis, valve regurgitation, arrhythmias and, later, myocardial infarction from aneurysm thrombosis or stenosis. Periungual desquamation and thrombocytosis typically appear in the second to third week.

Investigations: FBC (leucocytosis and anaemia early, thrombocytosis later), CRP and ESR, liver function (raised transaminases, low albumin), urinalysis (sterile pyuria), cultures and viral tests to exclude mimics, and an ECG. Echocardiography is essential at diagnosis and is repeated during follow-up, typically around 2 and 6 weeks, to detect coronary dilatation.

Management: give intravenous immunoglobulin promptly, ideally within 10 days of fever onset, together with aspirin. Aspirin is anti-inflammatory in the acute phase and is then continued as an antiplatelet agent. This is a recognised exception to avoiding aspirin in children because of Reye's syndrome; avoid concurrent influenza or varicella exposure, and consider influenza vaccination. Children at high risk of IVIG resistance or coronary involvement, or with persistent fever after IVIG, may receive corticosteroids or other immunomodulatory therapy under specialist guidance. Live vaccines are deferred for several months after IVIG, because the antibodies can impair the response. If aneurysms develop, long-term cardiology follow-up and antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy may be needed. Explain the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up plan clearly to his parents.

questions.q: "In a febrile child under 5, the height of the temperature is the best guide to the likelihood of serious bacterial infection." Critically evaluate this statement with reference to clinical assessment tools, specific age groups and illustrative conditions.

questions.modelAnswer:
Serious bacterial infections in young children include meningitis, septicaemia, pneumonia, urinary tract infection and bone and joint infection. They are uncommon in febrile children but cause substantial morbidity.

The statement holds most strongly in young infants. NICE NG143 treats any infant under 3 months with a temperature of 38 °C or more as high risk, and an infant aged 3–6 months with 39 °C or more as at least intermediate risk. In these age groups, the immature immune system and non-specific signs mean fever alone justifies careful assessment, and often a septic screen.

Beyond early infancy, the height of fever is a weak discriminator. Common viral infections such as influenza, roseola and adenovirus often cause high fevers, while a child with early meningococcal septicaemia may have only a modest temperature. Neonates and young infants with serious infection may be hypothermic or have no fever at all. NICE also advises that the response to antipyretics should not be used to distinguish bacterial from viral illness.

Structured assessment performs better. The traffic-light system combines colour, activity, respiratory signs, circulation and hydration, and other features. Red flags include pallor or mottling, failure to respond to social cues or difficulty rousing, grunting, a markedly raised respiratory rate, reduced skin turgor, a non-blanching rash, a bulging fontanelle, neck stiffness, focal neurology and seizures. Parental concern and clinician gestalt are also valuable.

Duration also matters. A fever lasting 5 days or more should prompt consideration of Kawasaki disease, where delay risks coronary aneurysms. Urinary tract infection in infants often presents with only fever and non-specific features, so urine testing is advised in an unexplained fever. Meningococcal disease can progress within hours from a non-specific febrile illness to shock, so the presence of a rash and the child's circulatory status matter far more than the temperature reading.

In conclusion, the statement is simplistic. Temperature is an essential input, and decisive in infants under 6 months, but the best guide to serious bacterial infection is the overall clinical picture: age, physiological red flags, duration, focal signs and the child's trajectory over time with clear safety-netting.
